https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government waives farm fees, expands cancer screening and bans circus animals The government also made decisions on strengthening the independence of the agricultural chamber, the election process for the president and deputies of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), measures to ensure the transparency of public funds, free driving licence acquisition for those in child protection care, and the establishment of a more effective screening system for cancer — government spokespersons announced at a press conference on Friday. Government spokesperson Anita Köböl stated that due to natural disasters in recent times — such as nationwide frost damage and drought, as well as livestock epidemics — the government supports an individual parliamentary motion under which the chamber may waive the collection of membership fees. This step amounts to an overall relief of approximately 18.6 billion forints for more than 400,000 producers, Anita Köböl highlighted. She added that, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, the funds are available, so this assistance does not jeopardise the balance of the budget. The government spokesperson also said that, in the government’s view, Hungarian agriculture is in immediate need of liquidity assistance and long-term protection. By the end of July, damage reports had been submitted for more than 768,000 hectares, which is more than double last year’s figure. She noted that, due to pressure on purchase prices, dairy farmers have also found themselves in a persistently difficult situation. For this reason, she announced, the agricultural minister has been tasked by the government with developing a comprehensive, long-term agricultural strategy. He indicated that the ministry will assist farmers who have suffered unprecedented elemental damage in 2026 by using available resources to pay out a so-called super advance. Instead of the usual mid-October date, payments will be launched as early as September, and the advance rate will be raised from 70 percent to 75 percent. Anita Köböl also reported that the cabinet had decided to further strengthen the transparency of public spending. She said that one of the conditions for accessing the resources of the European Union’s recovery fund is that public bodies involved in using these funds must proactively publish this data in a central registry. She indicated that the decision will expand the range of those obligated to publish and the data required to be disclosed, which will be freely accessible to anyone. “The use of public funds must be made traceable for everyone. Citizens have the right to know who the state is contracting with, what it is spending money on, and who receives the amounts paid from public funds,” she said. Anita Köböl also spoke about the government having instructed the Minister of Health to establish a far more effective and broader screening system accessible to all. The government spokesperson explained that a significant proportion of cancer deaths could be prevented, and a screening system that functions better, more accurately, and more predictably could save thousands of Hungarians every year. However, the latest data show that the participation rate of the Hungarian population in organised screening programmes is not only low but is continuously declining. She stressed that the government had therefore adopted a proposal on the review of the public health screening system and the preparation of its development. The Minister of Health and the Prime Minister will also take part in the available screenings in order to lead by example, she added. The acquisition, breeding, keeping, training, exhibition, and use of certain defined wild animal species and their hybrids in circus performances will be prohibited after 1 January 2027, government spokesperson Éva Magyar announced. She explained that in recent years there had been increasingly strong societal and animal welfare expectations that wild animals should not be used in circus productions. The trend across Europe is also clear, with member states restricting or banning the use of wild animals in circuses, she stressed. He touched on the fact that Hungary had previously applied only a partial ban, which had allowed animals from countries with stricter regulations to be brought into Hungarian menageries. He described the decision as justified on both animal welfare and safety grounds, pointing out that the keeping, transportation, training, and public performance of wild animals is incompatible with modern animal welfare standards and can also pose a risk of accidents. The regulation provides a fair transition: animals lawfully kept at the time of entry into force may continue to be kept for the rest of their lives or for as long as they remain part of the menagerie, but may not be bred, trained, displayed, or used in circus performances, the government spokesperson stated. Photograph: Joe Daniel Price/Getty Images New York New York City police fatally shoot man who climbed up Brooklyn Bridge cables Officers clipped to bridge had tried to talk man, who was holding a knife, into coming down safely, officials say Anna Betts Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.25 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New York City police shot and killed a man on Friday morning after he climbed on to the cables of the Brooklyn Bridge and approached officers with a knife extended, New York police department officials said. At a news conference on Friday, NYPD officials said that a 911 call came in at around 3.28am on Friday morning, reporting that a man was walking on the beams of the Brooklyn Bridge. Officers with the NYPD’s emergency service unit (ESU) responded to the scene, and saw a man “walking on the bridge cables”, Gerald Dowling, the commanding officer of ESU, told reporters. “Members of ESU climbed on to those cables and attempted to establish a verbal dialogue with the male and safely remove him from the bridge,” Dowling said. Dowling noted that the officers spent almost an hour speaking with the man, explaining that they were there to help, and tried to convince him to get down from the bridge safely. During the interaction, the officers observed that the man was holding a knife, he said. The man told the officers: “I want to die, I want you to kill me. I have a bomb. You are not going to make me do something bad to the cops.” Throughout the interaction, Dowling said, the officers continued trying to convince him to get down safely, while also issuing “multiple verbal commands for him to drop the knife”. After about an hour, hundreds of feet above the East River, the man “began to quickly descend the cable of the bridge towards the officers”, Dowling said, adding that at the time, the officers were still clipped to the bridge and positioned below the man on the same cable. Dowling said that when ESU officers are “conducting high-angle rescue”, they wear safety gear, including a harness, which is “physically clipped into the bridge” for their safety and noted that “being secured to the bridge drastically impacts the speed of their movement”. “The officers began to move backwards away from the male, but they were not able to move as quickly as the subject who was approaching them,” Dowling said. “When the male got within approximately 3ft from the closest member of ESU, he raised his arm with the knife extended outward towards the officer.” At that point, Dowling said, an ESU officer “who was on the roadbed of the bridge discharged his weapon one time, striking the male”. Dowling said that the officers then brought the male down from the cable and began rendering aid. The man was transported to a local hospital where he was pronounced deceased. A knife and a flashlight were recovered from the scene. Officials said that the entire incident was captured on police-worn body cameras. On social media, the police shared a photo of what they said was the knife recovered from the scene. The police have not yet released details regarding the identity of the man. “This incident is being investigated by the force investigation division,” Dowling said. “Members of ESU are specially trained for these types of high-risk and incredibly dangerous situations. They receive extensive instruction on de-escalation and how to engage with individuals compassionately.” The shooting came several days after police shot and killed a woman in Times Square after she attacked two people with knives, killing a 32-year-old woman . Sign up here Martin Belam Wed 11 Nov 2026 07.04 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 07.30 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. House Republicans have blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth . The defense secretary dismissed the impeachment resolution from a Republican lawmaker as “political spectacle”, saying it was an attempt to set up a “show trial” . Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Thomas Massie’s 34-page resolution, which he read aloud on the House floor, centered on the Iran war. Hegseth said the articles targeted not just him but the troops who carried out his orders. He insisted that every operation the articles cite – including strikes on Iran and Yemen, attacks on alleged drug boats and the capture of Venezuela’s now former leader Nicolás Maduro – was lawful, ordered by Donald Trump and notified to Congress. Why has the US Treasury chief reportedly moved? Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times reported. Bessent has led ‌the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, called Operation Economic Outcast, since August. Republicans elect Jim Jordan as House minority leader after midterm defeats View image in fullscreen Ohio lawmaker Jim Jordan is known for being a strident defender of Donald Trump. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA Republicans have elected the longtime congressman Jim Jordan as their new leader in the House of Representatives, putting a strident defender of Donald Trump at the helm of their conference as they navigate the fallout from sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections. Joseph Gedeon has this profile of the pugnacious Trump ideologue . We also have a gallery of newly elected Democrats , including Abdul El-Sayed and Annie Andrews, arriving in Washington for a new-member orientation day. Democrats demand answers on 8-year-old Haitian boy detained by ICE View image in fullscreen There are concerns about the whereabouts of the child who Democrats in California said was put in restraints and taken into custody last week. Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty Images Democratic lawmakers in California are demanding answers from the Trump administration about the safety and whereabouts of an eight-year-old Haitian boy who they say was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in last week. A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”. Fresh concerns raised over Gaza doctor held by Israel for 23 months without charge View image in fullscreen Dr Hussam Abu Safiya was detained at work in December 2024 and later held in solitary confinement at a notorious underground prison. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a prominent Gaza doctor held in an Israeli prison without charge for nearly 23 months has raised serious concerns about his health . Hussam Abu Safiya was detained at work in December 2024 and later held in solitary confinement at Rakefet, a notorious underground prison. During a visit by a lawyer from Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) last summer, the doctor told of harsh conditions, untreated medical problems and severe food shortages. British celebrity accused of using status to prey on young women for sex View image in fullscreen The allegations, which David Walliams denies, were revealed in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Composite: Guardian Design/ITV/REX/Shutterstock One of Britain’s best-known entertainers and children’s authors, David Walliams, has been accused of using his celebrity status to prey on young women for sex . The allegations, which he denies, were revealed in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News that spoke to 30 first-hand sources. A court rejected Walliams’s attempt to block publication after his legal team argued it was “highly likely” to lead him to attempt suicide. Michael Savage explains the main legal issues considered by the court – balancing Walliams’s right to privacy against the media’s right to publish. The full investigation is available here . In other news … View image in fullscreen Thomas Markle has been jailed after US authorities said he cut off a monitoring tag days after his arrest. Photograph: MEGA/GC Images The estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, has been jailed after US authorities said he cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units. At least three people are dead and three critically injured after a car struck pedestrians on a Los Angeles street corner during rush hour. The driver, whose identity remains unknown, is in a critical condition in hospital. The FDA has issued a new warning on GLP-1 weight-loss medications over a rare eye condition that could lead to sudden and permanent blindness. Parents are suing to stop a Washington state trans sports ban that could require “invasive” genital exams. An 11-month-old boy was found alive in South ⁠Carolina after he was believed to have been buried for ⁠about 24 hours , local police said. A woman in Saudi Arabia has been sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage. Climate check: Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans View image in fullscreen Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialized nations by 2035. Photograph: Bianca Otero/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance. Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialized nations by 2035 to help them cope with the effects of extreme weather and shift to a low-carbon future. But many rich governments have not yet set out their targets. You can follow the latest from Cop31 in Turkey with our live blog . Last Thing: Gilded statue in DC mocks Trump for ‘dodging’ Vietnam war draft over bone spurs View image in fullscreen The art installation entitled The Foot Soldier, was created by a group of anonymous artists known as the Secret Handshake. Photograph: mpi34/MediaPunch/Shutterstock A new statue titled The Foot Soldier mocking Donald Trump has been installed on Washington’s National Mall , this time poking fun at bone spurs he was diagnosed with, which allowed him to defer the Vietnam war draft. Created by the Secret Handshake, a group of anonymous artists, the statue depicts the US president sitting down while rubbing his bare foot.
